content: Primary amenorrhea refers to the absence of menstruation in a girl who has not yet started her monthly periods by the age of 15, despite having undergone other normal pubertal changes. A girl with primary amenorrhea will not experience menstrual bleeding, and this may or may not be accompanied by other signs of puberty. The menstrual cycle is regulated by hormones, and disruptions in these hormones can lead to primary amenorrhea. These disruptions may occur due to issues in the brain regions responsible for hormone production or due to ovarian dysfunction. The underlying causes of these problems can include genetic defects, infections (either in utero or after birth), congenital abnormalities, or tumors. In many cases, the exact cause of primary amenorrhea remains unknown. Conditions associated with primary amenorrhea include: Adrenogenital syndrome Anorexia nervosa Chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome or Sawyer syndrome Congenital heart disease (cyanotic) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Craniopharyngioma Chronic illnesses Cushing's disease Cystic fibrosis Gonadal dysgenesis Thyroid disorders (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism) Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Hyperprolactinemia Obesity Prader-Willi syndrome Polycystic ovarian disease Testicular feminization True hermaphroditism Tumors of the pituitary or adrenal glands Ovarian tumors Most girls begin menstruating between the ages of 9 and 18, with an average onset around 12 years old. Primary amenorrhea is typically diagnosed when a girl is older than 15 and has not started menstruating, despite showing other signs of puberty. It can also occur in the absence of other pubertal signs. Structural abnormalities of the reproductive system, such as a missing uterus or vagina, vaginal septum, cervical stenosis, or an imperforate hymen, can also lead to primary amenorrhea. Parents or guardians should seek medical care if their daughter is older than 16 and has not started menstruating, or if she is 14 and shows no other signs of puberty. To diagnose primary amenorrhea, a healthcare provider will perform a physical examination and take a detailed medical history. A pregnancy test is typically conducted, and blood tests may be ordered to measure hormone levels, including estradiol, FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, T3, and T4. Additional tests may include: 17-hydroxyprogesterone Chromosome analysis Head CT or MRI scans Laparoscopy Pelvic ultrasound Progesterone withdrawal test Serum progesterone levels Treatment for primary amenorrhea depends on the underlying cause. If the condition is due to congenital abnormalities, treatment may involve hormone therapy, surgery, or both. For cases caused by a pituitary tumor, treatment options include medications to shrink the tumor, surgical removal, or radiation therapy if other treatments are ineffective. If systemic diseases are responsible, addressing the underlying condition may allow menstruation to begin. In cases of low body weight due to anorexia or excessive exercise, restoring normal weight or reducing exercise levels can often lead to the resumption of periods. The prognosis for primary amenorrhea depends on its cause. Conditions such as adrenogenital syndrome, chronic illness, congenital heart disease, drastic weight loss, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, imperforate hymen, malnutrition, delayed onset of puberty, obesity, or thyroid overactivity often have a good chance of being corrected with medication, lifestyle changes, or surgery. However, conditions like congenital abnormalities of the upper genital tract, craniopharyngioma, cystic fibrosis, gonadal dysgenesis, Prader-Willi syndrome, testicular feminization syndrome, true hermaphroditism, or Turner syndrome are less likely to resolve spontaneously. In cases where menstruation cannot be restored, medications can sometimes induce a menstrual-like state (pseudomenstruation). These treatments can help individuals feel more aligned with their peers and family and also protect against bone thinning (osteoporosis).
